title: Kingdom of Scotland

lead.label: Overview
lead.text: In 1600, James VI ruled a Scottish kingdom with its own crown, council and parliament. English and Scottish crowns were still separate.

organization.label: Government
organization.text: James VI worked with the Privy Council in the conduct of central government.

organization.label: Institutions
organization.text: Parliament’s estates sat together in one chamber. The Lords of the Articles prepared legislation; conventions of estates also dealt with taxation.

organization.label: Seat / capital
organization.text: No independently verified seat entry is admitted in this pilot.

organization.label: Administrative relationships
organization.text: Shire commissioners represented qualified lesser landholders. Royal burgh commissioners also coordinated through their own convention.
organization.scope: Arrangements established in 1587 and in operation by 1600

changes.text: Provision for shire commissioners broadened the mechanism of representation for lesser barons, though participation was uneven.
James began restoring bishops to the Church of Scotland. This was a developing policy, not an assertion that the later system already existed.

population.label: Population
population.text: No population observation is admitted for this entity and date.

overview.label: Royal and representative government
overview.text: The king and Privy Council handled the daily work of central government. Parliament met intermittently rather than as a permanent legislature. Royal authority and the estates operated together, but their relationship was not a modern separation of powers.

overview.label: Who represented the kingdom?
overview.text: Nobles, church interests, royal burghs and an emerging body of shire commissioners participated in parliamentary politics. The 1587 arrangements did not create universal suffrage. The royal burghs maintained a collective voice through a separate convention.
